salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, the hospitality minimum wage (National Minimum Wage) is $26.44 per hour, giving an annual gross of $52,265.44 before casual loading and super.

faqs.q: Does the hospitality minimum wage include casual loading?
faqs.a: No. The National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour does not include casual loading. Casual employees in hospitality are entitled to an additional 25% loading, making the casual minimum rate $33.05 per hour. Our timesheet has a checkbox to add casual loading on top of the base rate you enter.

faqs.q: How is super calculated on the hospitality minimum wage?
faqs.a: Superannuation guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top of your hourly rate. For a full-time employee on the minimum wage ($26.44/hour, 38 hours/week), the employer contributes an extra $6,271.85 per year, up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Casual loading is also ordinary earnings, so super applies to the loaded rate.

faqs.q: What tax would I pay on the hospitality minimum wage?
faqs.a: Using the 2026–27 resident tax scale, a full-time employee earning $52,265.44 gross pays no tax on the first $18,200, 15% on the next $26,800, and 30% on the remaining $7,265.44, plus a 2% Medicare levy. Estimated tax and Medicare is about $6,900, leaving around $45,365 take-home. Use our take-home pay guide for a detailed estimate.

bodyMarkdown:
## Hospitality Minimum Wage: From Hourly Rate to Annual Salary

If you work in hospitality or are considering a job offer, understanding how your hourly rate translates to annual pay is essential. The **hospitality minimum wage** is a common starting point, but casual loading, superannuation, and tax all affect your real income. This guide explains the conversion, using the National Minimum Wage as a base, and shows how to use our [timesheet](/) to calculate your own figures.

### The Basic Formula: Hourly × Hours × 52

Annual gross pay is calculated as:

**Hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week (the standard under the Fair Work Act), the formula becomes:

**Hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour. Multiply by 38 hours gives $1,004.90 per week, and by 52 weeks gives $52,265.44 per year. This is before any casual loading, penalty rates, or super.

### Casual Loading: 25% on Top

Many hospitality jobs are casual. Casual employees receive a 25% loading instead of paid leave. The casual minimum rate is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When using our [timesheet](/), you enter your base hourly rate (e.g., $26.44) and tick the “Add 25% casual loading” checkbox. **Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – the tool adds it for you.

For a casual on the hospitality minimum wage, the annual gross becomes $65,331.80 ($33.05 × 38 × 52). That’s a significant difference.

### Award Rates vs. National Minimum Wage

The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor. Most hospitality employees are covered by the Hospitality Industry General Award, which sets higher minimum rates for classifications like food and beverage attendant, cook, or manager. Award rates vary by level and age. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award. Always check your award rate – it may be higher than the national minimum.

### Fortnightly Pay: A Common Schedule

Many hospitality employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross, multiply your weekly pay by 2. For a full-time permanent employee on $26.44/hour: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80 per fortnight. For a casual: $1,291.50 × 2 = $2,583.00 per fortnight. Knowing your fortnightly amount helps with budgeting and comparing job offers.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Employers must pay superannuation guarantee of 12% on your ordinary earnings. This is paid on top of your hourly rate – it is not deducted from your pay. For a full-time permanent employee on the minimum wage, the employer contributes an extra $6,271.85 per year (12% of $52,265.44). For a casual on $33.05/hour, super is 12% of $65,331.80 = $7,839.82 per year. Super stops once your earnings exceed the maximum contribution base of $270,830 (2026–27).

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your annual gross is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies progressive tax rates and the Medicare levy (generally 2%). For 2026–27, the tax-free threshold is $18,200. For a full-time permanent employee on $52,265.44, estimated tax and Medicare is about $6,900, leaving around $45,365 take-home. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a personalised estimate. Note: this estimate does not include HELP repayments, Medicare levy surcharge, or salary sacrifice.

### Industry Average vs. Your Job

The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports average weekly earnings for accommodation and food services as $1,509.90 per week (full-time ordinary time, May 2026). That is an **industry average**, not a median for your specific job. Your actual pay depends on your award classification, experience, and location. For a more accurate picture, refer to [job pay](/topics/job-pay) resources or your award.

### Using Our Timesheet

Our [timesheet](/) is the home page. Enter your base hourly rate (e.g., $26.44), select your hours per week (default 38), and tick casual loading if applicable. The tool shows your weekly, fortnightly, and annual gross, plus estimated super and tax. It does not include penalty rates or allowances – those are separate.

### Key Distinctions

- **National Minimum Wage**: $26.44/hour (permanent), $33.05/hour (casual with 25% loading).
- **Award rates**: Often higher; check your award.
- **Casual loading**: 25% on top of base rate, paid as part of hourly rate.
- **Super**: 12% paid on top of ordinary earnings, including casual loading.
- **Tax**: Progressive rates plus Medicare levy.

### Disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more details, see our [reference tables](/data) and [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page.
